nature-pol-018.title: Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems
nature-pol-018.text: In 1863, after harmful chemical releases caused health problems, the UK adopted the Alkali Act and created the Alkali Inspectorate. It was an early example of environmental policy: a commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems. Such policy typically covers air and water pollution, waste, the management of ecosystems, biodiversity, resources from nature and endangered species. Its aim is to steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people. Why should government get involved at all? The usual answer is {{ref:nature-found-045}}, such as the free rider problem and the tragedy of the commons. Some problems spur action faster than others. Pollution of air and water tends to move governments more than global warming does, because it causes immediate health problems. Success is judged by how far a policy reduces or solves environmental problems, and whether policies have done so remains debated.

nature-pol-027.title: Market-based instruments: using prices to cut pollution
nature-pol-027.text: David Lloyd George's fuel tax of 1909-1910 may have been Britain's first market-based environmental instrument. Such instruments are policy tools that use markets, prices and other economic signals to give polluters a reason to cut harmful side effects such as pollution. They are also called economic instruments, price-based instruments or new policy instruments for the environment. They tackle the market failure of an {{ref:nature-found-031}} in two ways. They charge for external costs through taxes, or they create property rights and a market for using environmental services. Examples include environmental taxes, charges and subsidies, emissions trading, deposit-refund systems, eco-labeling laws and property rights; the EU's emissions trading scheme is one. They differ from voluntary agreements and from command-and-control rules that dictate performance or technology, though they usually still need some regulation. Environmental advocates first opposed them. After successful credit trading in the US lead phasedown, they came to support trading, starting with the acid rain allowance market.

nature-pol-030.title: Public choice: politics without romance
nature-pol-030.text: James Buchanan described public choice as 'politics without romance'. It uses economic tools such as rational choice and {{ref:nature-econ-034}} to study how politicians, officials and voters behave and interact. It stresses that political agents are self-interested, and that collective decisions combine many individual choices. It doubts that government simply maximizes social welfare. Instead it models officials who may also act for their own benefit, as in the budget-maximizing model of bureaucracy. Duncan Black, sometimes called its founding father, laid the groundwork for median voter theory in papers from 1948 to 1958. Its Nobel laureates include Kenneth Arrow, James Buchanan, George Stigler, Gary Becker, Amartya Sen, Vernon Smith and {{ref:nature-hist-039}}. It has critics. Steven Pressman argues it fails to explain key political behavior, such as why politicians vote against their constituents' interests, or indeed why people vote.

nature-pol-042.title: Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth
nature-pol-042.text: Robert Shiller's classic example is a landowner who chains a river and charges passing boats to lower the chain. The landowner adds no value. That is rent-seeking. It means increasing one's wealth by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth. 'Rent' here means {{ref:nature-res-218}}: income beyond what is needed to keep a factor in its current use. Profit-seeking creates wealth through mutually beneficial trade; rent-seeking only redistributes existing wealth. Typical examples are lobbying for subsidies, tariffs, quotas or rules that hobble competitors. The costs are broad. Rent-seeking wastes resources, stifles competition, lowers wealth creation and government revenue, and raises inequality and corruption risk. Money spent on lobbyists rather than research or equipment slows growth, and Mancur Olson argued that countries dominated by organized interest groups lose vitality and decline. Critics note it can be hard to tell beneficial profit-seeking from harmful rent-seeking.

nature-pol-044.title: The logic of collective action: why small groups win
nature-pol-044.text: In 1965 Mancur Olson's book The Logic of Collective Action argued that small groups with concentrated interests win out over large groups with diffuse interests. The reason is the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Members of any group providing a public good are tempted to free ride on others' efforts. Large groups face higher organizing costs, and each member gains less, so they are less able to act. Without selective incentives, collective action is unlikely even among large groups with shared interests. A minority bound by concentrated incentives can therefore dominate the majority. Critics dispute parts of the argument. Susanne Lohmann notes the US quota on sugar imports ({{ref:nature-pol-005}}) created 2,261 jobs while reducing overall welfare, and blames information asymmetry rather than free riding. Gunnar Trumbull counters that diffuse interests such as consumers can win through a 'legitimacy premium' and coalitions.

nature-pol-026.title: Induced innovation: expensive inputs spur new inventions
nature-pol-026.text: John Hicks proposed an idea in The Theory of Wages in 1932. When one input becomes relatively more expensive, firms are spurred to invent ways of using less of it. This is induced innovation. The classic illustration is higher wages encouraging labor-saving inventions. The idea has been applied to rising energy costs speeding up energy efficiency. Global GDP and CO2 emissions grew together until the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises cut consumption. After the oil shock, investment in alternative energy, efficient cars and heating meant CO2 grew more slowly than GDP, even after petrol prices fell in the 1980s. Farming shows the same pattern: when scarce inputs such as land rise in price, farmers seek technologies that use more abundant inputs instead. Not every model captures it. The DICE climate model treats innovation as external, so it leaves out induced technological change.

nature-pol-025.title: Implicit carbon prices: charging for carbon without saying so
nature-pol-025.text: Almost every country taxes gasoline, but only 39 have explicit carbon pricing. A fuel tax is an implicit carbon price. It puts a cost on greenhouse gas emissions indirectly, through a measure that changes the cost of emitting without targeting carbon itself. Explicit carbon prices, such as carbon taxes and emissions trading, target emissions directly. Implicit and explicit prices together make the effective carbon price. Implicit prices can also be negative. Fuel taxes raise the cost of emitting, but fossil fuel subsidies make emitting cheaper. Implicit prices spread more easily, because they tackle local problems, need less administrative capacity and face less political opposition. The difference matters at borders. The EU's border carbon adjustment counts only explicit prices, while a proposed US version would include implicit ones.

nature-pol-024.title: Gossen's second law: getting the most from a budget
nature-pol-024.text: Gossen's second law is named after Hermann Heinrich Gossen (1810–1858). It says a person gets the most from a budget by spending so that the extra satisfaction per unit of money is equal across all goods. Suppose the last unit of money spent on one good bought less extra satisfaction than it could have bought elsewhere. Then the person would do better to switch. Formally, the law follows from maximizing utility under a {{ref:nature-econ-102}} with Lagrange multipliers.

nature-pol-198.title: Counting fossil fuel subsidies: why the totals differ
nature-pol-198.text: In 2021 the UK government said it did not subsidize fossil fuels under the IEA definition, while others said it did under the OECD definition. The dispute is over definitions. Estimates add up payments, compare prices with world prices, and may count health and climate damage. Counting unpriced damage makes IMF estimates far larger than those using OECD and International Energy Agency definitions. One IMF paper found underpricing of local air pollution was the largest part of global subsidies, at 42%, followed by global warming costs at 29%. The fiscal cost of government support for fossil fuels was 1.1 trillion USD in 2023, 90% of it tied to consumption.

nature-pol-001.title: International trade: goods, money and pollution across borders
nature-pol-001.text: In 2025 world trade totaled 80,733 billion US dollars, of which merchandise made up 52,865 billion. International trade is the exchange of capital, goods and services across national borders to meet a need or demand. A product sold from one country to another is an export for the seller's country and an import for the buyer's. Trade abroad is usually costlier than trade at home, because of tariffs and other barriers such as border delays, language and legal differences. It also substitutes for moving inputs. Capital and labor move less easily between countries, so a country can instead import goods that embody them. Mineral fuels and oils were the top traded commodity by export value in 2022. Organizations such as the {{ref:nature-pol-007}} work to ease and expand trade. Trade also ties countries to distant environments. A 2020 study of 189 countries found most are more exposed to over-exploited water, energy and land resources through trade, mainly from distant sources.

nature-pol-007.title: The World Trade Organization: referee of world trade
nature-pol-007.text: Without the World Trade Organization, studies find, the average country would face tariffs on its exports 32 percentage points higher. The WTO is the intergovernmental organization that regulates and eases trade between countries. Its forerunner, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), was set up by 23 countries in 1947 and concentrated on cutting tariffs. The Marrakesh Agreement, signed on 15 April 1994, established the WTO, which began on 1 January 1995. It has 166 members and 23 observer governments. It provides a forum for negotiations and settling disputes, reviews national trade policies and helps poorer countries adjust to its rules. It sets the rules of trade policy rather than outcomes. The Doha Round, launched in 2001 to make globalization help the world's poor, stalled over farm subsidies, industrial tariffs and other barriers. Its director-general has called for reform, including on global public goods such as climate protection.

nature-pol-011.title: The global waste trade: shipping rubbish across borders
nature-pol-011.text: Waste mostly flows from the Global North to be disposed of in the Global South. The global waste trade ships it between countries for treatment, disposal or recycling. Richer, more urbanized countries produce more solid waste, and developing countries often import toxic or hazardous waste from developed ones. Scholars link the trade's sharp growth to the free-market policies of the 1980s, which pushed developing countries to import waste as a route to economic expansion. Supporters argue it can stimulate economies with little else to offer the global economy. Critics see dumping. Most hazardous waste is produced in the United States and Europe, yet the health harms fall on poorer countries. Lacking safe facilities, people there handle toxic waste by hand, and poor disposal causes illness and death. Dump sites carry heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants that kill birds, fish and other wildlife. The trade is hard to regulate, since vague definitions let hazardous waste be exported as commodities or raw materials.

nature-pol-002.title: Local or imported: which is greener?
nature-pol-002.text: Buying local sounds green, but the evidence is mixed. Studies find food miles, the distance food travels, are a relatively minor source of carbon emissions. Localizing food may still allow energy, water and nutrients to be reused. Seasons complicate the picture. Different harvest seasons can make importing from far away greener than local storage or greenhouse growing. There are hard limits too. A 2020 study found local crops within 100 km could not meet demand for most food crops for 72-89% of the world's population. Regional differences make some places better suited to a product, which favors trade, and local production may need policies such as eco-tariffs to compete. Jobs are disputed as well. One study found trade can raise local employment; another found import exposure cut local employment and labor income. Researchers still disagree on the environmental and employment trade-offs.

nature-pol-003.title: Non-tariff barriers: trade limits beyond taxes
nature-pol-003.text: A 2019 UNCTAD report found that trade costs from non-tariff measures were more than double those of traditional tariffs. Non-tariff barriers are restrictions on imports or exports other than tariffs, such as quotas, licenses, subsidies, customs delays and technical standards. As tariffs fell through GATT and WTO negotiation rounds, protectionism turned to new measures such as technical barriers to trade. They are grouped as protectionist, assistance (such as domestic subsidies) or non-protectionist, the last aimed at health, safety and the environment. Most can be called protectionist unless they address market problems such as externalities or information asymmetries, as safety standards and labels do. Rising consumer demand for safe and environmentally friendly products has made technical barriers more popular. Whether a particular measure protects health and environment or disguises protectionism is often disputed.

nature-pol-008.title: Green exceptions in trade rules
nature-pol-008.text: Trade rules do not forbid every limit on imports. WTO agreements let governments, in specific circumstances, restrict trade to protect the environment and public, animal and plant health. The condition is that members must not use such measures to disguise protectionist policies. The Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures governs quarantine rules for pests and diseases. The line is tested in disputes. In 2006 the WTO ruled that the European Union broke trade law between 1999 and 2003 with its moratorium on approving imports of genetically modified organisms. The {{ref:nature-gov-044}} states that trade and environment agreements should be mutually supportive. In 2024 US Democrats argued that a carbon border adjustment is a fee permissible under WTO rules, not a carbon tax.

nature-pol-010.title: Has the WTO delivered? The critics' case
nature-pol-010.text: Ha-Joon Chang notes that developing countries grew faster in 1960–1980 than in 1980–2000, even though their trade policies are now far more liberal. Critics say the gains from WTO-backed free trade are not shared equally, pointing to widening gaps between rich and poor. They fear early liberalizing traps developing economies in the primary sector, which often needs little skilled labor. Vietnam cut poverty and grew fast while liberalizing slowly with safeguards; El Salvador's growth stayed weak after it removed import barriers and cut tariffs. Studies credit the WTO with boosting trade, but whether liberalizing reliably brings growth remains disputed.

nature-pol-009.title: Equal terms for all: the WTO's non-discrimination rule
nature-pol-009.text: The WTO's non-discrimination rule has two parts. Most-favored-nation treatment means the best terms a member gives any WTO member for a product must be given to all members. Exceptions include free trade agreements and preferential treatment for developing countries. National treatment means imports must be treated no less favorably than domestic goods once inside the market; it targets discriminatory technical standards. The WTO's other key principles are reciprocity, binding and enforceable commitments, transparency and safety valves.

nature-pol-006.title: The pollution haven hypothesis: do dirty industries flee strict rules?
nature-pol-006.text: After the US tightened lead air standards in 2009, exports of used lead-acid batteries to Mexico rose four-fold. More low-birth-weight babies followed near Mexican recycling plants. The pollution haven hypothesis holds that firms investing abroad move to countries with cheap resources and weak environmental rules, making them havens for pollution. The logic is cost. Stricter rules raise input costs for pollution-intensive goods and erode a place's {{ref:nature-econ-106}}. The claim comes in three strengths: pollution costs matter at the margin; they measurably shift trade and investment; or countries deliberately set standards too low to attract investment. The first two have empirical support. How much the effect matters next to other trade and investment factors remains disputed. It may partly explain the {{ref:nature-eecon-225}}, as polluting industry shifts from richer to poorer economies.

nature-pol-004.title: When green standards keep out foreign goods
nature-pol-004.text: Product standards on labeling, testing and composition protect health and the environment, but they can also keep out foreign goods. Standards enacted for health and safety can serve protectionist and political ends. The mechanism is subtle. Tariffs raise marginal costs and grow with volume, while testing or labeling rules impose fixed costs. Fixed compliance costs can push small exporters out while leaving large multinationals untouched, shifting profits toward them. This logic explains why large chemical producers supported the EU's REACH regulation. Some barriers are not protectionist at all, such as import bans based on objectionable harvesting or fishing methods.

nature-pol-017.title: The Bamako Convention: Africa bans imported hazardous waste
nature-pol-017.text: In 1991 African nations, unhappy with the Basel Convention, signed the Bamako Convention. It goes further, banning imports of all hazardous waste generated outside the Organization of African Unity and treating imports from non-parties as illegal. Its reach was very limited, though. With scarce resources and weak enforcement, members could not stop toxic dumping. The Lomé IV Convention similarly banned exports of hazardous wastes from the European Community to African, Caribbean and Pacific states.

nature-pol-012.title: The economic case for exporting waste
nature-pol-012.text: In a 1991 memo, Lawrence Summers, then World Bank chief economist, wrote that the economic logic of dumping toxic waste in the lowest-wage country was 'impeccable'. The memo called countries in Africa 'vastly under polluted'. It asked whether the World Bank should encourage dirty industries to move to the least developed countries. A Cato Institute article argued that people in developing countries would rationally accept more exposure to pollutants for higher productivity and income. The case rests mainly on their need for economic development. Critics call the practice toxic colonialism.

nature-pol-014.title: The e-waste trade: rich countries' old electronics
nature-pol-014.text: An estimated 50 million tons of e-waste are produced each year, mostly in the United States and Europe, and most is shipped to Asia and Africa for processing and recycling. The trade grows with fast technological change, falling prices and {{ref:nature-eecon-188}}. Heavy metals and toxins leak into waterways and groundwater. They expose dump workers, children searching for items to sell and nearby residents. In Guiyu, China, possibly the world's largest e-waste dump, workers dismantle over 1.5 million pounds of junked electronics a year.

nature-pol-016.title: The plastic waste trade: exporting marine litter
nature-pol-016.text: In 2018 Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte threatened war unless Canada took back 64 tonnes of garbage, shipped by a plastic-recycling firm and mislabeled as recyclable. The international trade in waste plastics has been identified as the main cause of marine litter. Countries importing them often lack the capacity to process it all. The United Nations therefore restricts trade in plastic waste unless it meets certain criteria.

nature-pol-015.title: Shipbreaking: dismantling old ships in Asia
nature-pol-015.text: Industrialized countries increasingly send old ships to Asia to be dismantled, because it is cheaper there. China and Bangladesh are the two hubs of shipbreaking. The ships were built under weaker environmental rules and contain asbestos, lead oxide, mercury, arsenic and tributyltin. Workers traditionally handle these substances without proper equipment or protective gear.

nature-pol-013.title: Toxic colonialism: poorer countries as dumping grounds
nature-pol-013.text: Toxic colonialism is the use of poorer countries as cheap places to export or dump the hazardous waste of developed countries. It is the core critique of the global waste trade. The word 'colonialism' fits, critics say, because economic dependence, exploitation of labor and cultural inequality mark both. T.V. Reed links it to colonial views of indigenous land as empty 'waste', which make Global South land seem expendable for Western wastes. Laura Pratt argues agreements have not stopped it, because waste moves under false permits, bribes, improper labels or the pretext of recycling.

nature-pol-005.title: Import quotas: capping what crosses the border
nature-pol-005.text: An import quota is a limit, by value or quantity, on how much of a good may be imported or exported over a period. Quotas usually raise costs, narrow consumers' choice and raise import prices for companies. 'Voluntary' export restraints are limits an exporter accepts under threat of sanctions. Embargoes are the extreme case: an outright ban on trade in certain goods.

openers.trade-and-the-environment: In 2025 world trade was worth 80,733 billion US dollars, and it carries environmental costs and choices across borders. The World Trade Organization, formed in 1995, sets the rules, and lets countries restrict trade to protect the environment and health as long as the measures are not disguised protectionism. Standards and labels can protect people yet also keep out foreign goods. Some fear firms move to countries with weak rules, turning them into havens for pollution. And waste itself is traded, often from rich countries to poor ones, a practice a 1991 memo by Lawrence Summers famously defended.

reviews.trade-and-the-environment: Trade links every country to environments far away, and the rules of the World Trade Organization decide how far governments may restrict it for health and nature. Green standards and other barriers sit on a thin line between protection and protectionism, and fixed compliance costs can favor large firms over small exporters. Stricter rules at home may push pollution abroad, as lead batteries sent to Mexico showed. The waste trade makes the pattern plain: hazardous waste, e-waste, plastics and old ships flow to poorer countries, defended as rational development and condemned as toxic colonialism.
